title: Two cities
hook: we belong to two commonwealths: our town and the whole world (On Leisure 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: not wise, Seneca's confession that he never will be. Your line was less bad each day. Which fault did you take a sliver from? Day five hundred eleven, the end of a week.

Fill in a form and it asks where you're from. A city, a state, a country. A box with room for one answer. But think about what actually shapes your days: news from the other side of the planet, a cousin in another country, the same moon everyone sees, a sky that doesn't stop at a border. Seneca wrote a short book called On Leisure, and only part of it survives; its opening is lost. But the surviving part contains one of the biggest ideas in Stoic thought, and it fits into a single sentence about where you belong. Today: two cities.
screen: `WHERE ARE YOU FROM?` → `A BOX WITH ROOM FOR ONE.` → `A BOOK WITH ITS OPENING LOST.`

segments.voice: First, the two. Let's hold in our minds, Seneca writes, two commonwealths. One is great and truly shared, holding gods and humans alike, where we don't look to this corner or that, but measure our borders by the path of the sun. The other is the one the accident of birth assigned us: Athens, Carthage, wherever. It belongs to some people, not all. Second, serving both. Some people, Seneca says, serve both cities at once. Some serve only the small one, some only the great one. And here's his surprise: the great city can be served even in leisure, maybe best in leisure, by thinking clearly about how to live and passing it on. Third, an old idea with new reach. Long before Seneca, Diogenes, asked where he came from, is said to have answered: I'm a citizen of the world. The Greek word is kosmopolitēs, where we get cosmopolitan. The Stoics took up that idea and developed it in their own way: in some sense, every person, everywhere, is a fellow citizen. Fourth, both, not either. Seneca isn't telling anyone to abandon their town. You still owe your street, your neighbors, your local school. But you also belong to something with no border, and you owe it something too. And the week, looking back: the raised hand, my faults too, hard training, a worthy opponent, in agreement, less bad each day. Every one of them is practice for living in both cities at once.
screen: `ONE CITY BY BIRTH, ONE BY THE SUN.` · `SERVE BOTH, EVEN IN LEISURE.` · `DIOGENES: A CITIZEN OF THE WORLD.` · `BOTH, NOT EITHER.` · then, large: `TWO CITIES.`

segments.voice: Picture your small city: your street, your building, the shop on the corner, the people you nod to. Hold it for a few breaths. Now let the picture widen: your country, the continent, the whole curve of the planet in sunlight and shadow, billions of people waking and sleeping. You belong to both. Ask: what's one thing I could do this week for the small city? And one thing for the great one? Let an answer come for each. The bell holds the time.
Two cities. Seneca's picture in On Leisure: the town birth gave us, and the great commonwealth measured by the sun. We belong to both. Today's word.
Your line: two cities. Do one thing today for each: one for your street, one for the wider world. Small is fine. Day five hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often think of themselves as belonging both to their local community and to humanity as a whole, and look for ways to serve each.

fork.setup: you're retired from public life. can you still serve the great commonwealth, by Seneca's account?
options: yes, even in leisure, by thinking and passing it on.
fork.reveal: he says the great city can be served in leisure, perhaps even best there.

original.note: Greek, 'citizen of the world': Diogenes' answer, which the Stoics built on.

trapdoor: what you thought: cosmopolitan means sophisticated and well-traveled.
what it means: it means a citizen of the world; Seneca says we belong to two cities, our town and the whole.
what a scholar hears: On Leisure's beginning is lost and its addressee uncertain, likely Serenus; the two-commonwealth idea runs from Diogenes through Zeno's Republic to Marcus Aurelius.

notes: On Leisure 4.1–2 paraphrased: two commonwealths, one great and common to gods and men, measured by the sun; the other assigned by birth (Athens, Carthage); some serve both, some one; the greater can be served in leisure. Confirm.
Diogenes Laertius 6.63: 'I am a citizen of the world' (kosmopolitēs). Confirm.
On Leisure is incomplete (opening lost); addressee probably Serenus. Confirm.
Week look-back (days 505–510) uses those days' carries.
How directly Stoic cosmopolitanism grew from Diogenes' quip is debated; the teach now says the Stoics developed the idea in their own way rather than built a whole ethic on it.
